entry.title: CoreWeave bond yield rises above 16% amid increasing credit stress in AI infrastructure sector [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: CoreWeave's 2032 bond yield has surged past 16%, reflecting growing investor concern over financing risks in the AI data center market. Credit default swap costs have also increased for major AI-linked companies like Nvidia, Broadcom, and Oracle, signaling heightened default risk perceptions. The rise in credit costs comes amid political challenges and potential moratoriums on data center expansions in key states such as Texas, Ohio, and Georgia, which could delay or reduce AI infrastructure spending. Despite these pressures, AI-related debt issuance remains robust, with significant borrowing expected to continue funding hyperscaler capital expenditures. Market analysts warn that the sustainability of AI spending depends on future cash flow generation and timely monetization, with potential risks including delayed contracts and reduced capital expenditure. Forecasts suggest AI-related credit issuance may peak soon, with possible declines if infrastructure projects slow due to political or economic factors.

entry.title: Simon Willison uses Claude Code to build Beep Locator, a Python web app triangulating a mysterious beep in a room using multiple devices and browser microphones [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Simon Willison developed Beep Locator with Claude Code to identify the source of an intermittent beep in his house by triangulating sound using multiple devices like iPads, phones, and laptops connected via a Python web server. The system uses browser microphones and WebSockets to detect beeps, estimate device locations, and map the sound source to within about 40cm, ultimately locating a carbon monoxide detector needing new batteries. Beep Locator is based on the 2007 BeepBeep acoustic ranging system paper and runs a Python server coordinating devices that record audio buffers and detect beeps using Fast Fourier Transform and high-pass filters. The system aligns audio clips using chirps played by devices, supports manual rough positioning of devices, and includes features like clapping mode for testing and replaying recorded sounds to confirm the beep source. The project demonstrates how Claude Code can be extended with audio input capabilities by running JavaScript and Python code analyzing microphone data across devices, enabling remote live code updates and interactive debugging without manual intervention on each listener device.

entry.title: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with improved coding, reasoning, and vision capabilities, faster output, and enhanced safety features [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic has upgraded its Claude Fable and Claude Mythos models to version 5.2, enhancing their abilities in coding, reasoning, and vision tasks. These models have demonstrated success in complex technical challenges such as software migrations, device design, physics problem-solving, robotics, and formal mathematical proofs. Claude Fable 5.2 includes robust cybersecurity and biology safeguards, making it broadly available, while Mythos 5.2 is accessible through specialized programs for life sciences and cybersecurity research. The new versions communicate more clearly and generate outputs up to 30% faster than their predecessors, with an optional fast mode that increases speed by up to 2.5 times at higher pricing. Extensive prerelease safety testing indicates that these models maintain or improve alignment and safety measures, including protections against misuse and distillation attacks. Anthropic recommends using Claude Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, reserving Fable and Mythos 5.2 for more ambitious technical work or as advisors and orchestrators in multi-model workflows.

entry.title: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, highest among comparable models despite high cost and slow speed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Claude Fable 5.2, a proprietary AI model released in November 2026, achieved a score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, significantly above the median score of 40 for similar models. It supports text and image inputs with a 1 million token context window but is noted for its high cost and slower performance compared to peers. The model's pricing is $8.00 per 1 million input tokens and $40.00 per 1 million output tokens, making it more expensive than the median rates of $2.00 and $10.00 respectively. It also takes an average of 46.4 minutes per task, which is considerably slower than the median of 12.6 minutes. Claude Fable 5.2 is also very verbose, generating 275 million tokens during evaluation compared to a median of 72.8 million.

entry.title: Google confirms Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human reviewers despite earlier privacy promises [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Google has updated its policies to disclose that its Gemini AI system routes personal content from Gmail and Drive to human annotators, reversing its 2023 promise that such data would not be seen by humans. Testing shows that Gemini autonomously accesses and ingests personal files and emails during conversations without explicit user commands, sometimes including sensitive information in the review pipeline. The ingestion process is probabilistic, with outcomes ranging from no data retrieval to full unredacted file ingestion. Google warns users not to connect apps containing confidential information to Gemini, as automatic scrubbers cannot fully deidentify personal data. This change raises concerns about privacy and the extent of human review in AI-assisted Workspace integrations.

entry.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model for complex reasoning and agent tasks, offering higher intelligence per cost than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Meta introduced Muse Ember, a compact and efficient AI model designed for complex reasoning tasks such as tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. It delivers superior intelligence per dollar compared to Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, matching or exceeding their performance at significantly lower costs. Muse Ember is available via the Meta Model API with pricing set at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. The model supports a 1 million token context window and up to 512,000 output tokens, enabling it to process entire codebases or document sets in a single call. Early testing by partners highlighted its speed, accuracy, and efficiency in tasks like contract review, candidate screening, and coding, with latency significantly lower than comparable models. Muse Ember also natively understands multiple modalities including text, images, audio, and video, allowing it to handle diverse real-world inputs without separate models. Designed for high-throughput agentic workloads, Muse Ember excels at repetitive, structured tasks agents perform throughout the day. It is positioned as a cost-effective foundation for enterprise AI agents handling workflows end to end, and it can be paired with Meta's larger Muse Wonder model for more complex problem-solving.

entry.title: Research develops a prototype case-based reasoning system to enhance academic advising and potentially replace human advisors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This research explores the application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) to academic advising, a critical but time-consuming function in higher education. The study presents the design, development, and validation of a prototype CBR-based academic advisement recommender system intended to supplement traditional advising processes and improve their effectiveness and efficiency. The prototype aims to address the widespread need for improved advisement services in colleges and universities worldwide by leveraging CBR expert system methodologies, which have been successful in other problem-solving domains but have not yet been applied effectively to academic advising. The system could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors as its capabilities mature.

entry.title: Researchers introduce NormGym benchmark to evaluate AI agents' ability to infer and apply hidden social norms through interaction, finding current large language models achieve only 55.3% success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: NormGym is an interactive benchmark designed to test normative competence, where AI agents must infer hidden social norms while completing tasks in multi-agent environments. The benchmark challenges agents to distinguish permissible actions from possible ones by observing behaviors and sanctions within the community. Evaluation of current models, including large language models, shows that while they can sometimes adjust behavior after personal sanctions, they struggle to infer norms from others' actions and sanctions, with the best model achieving just over half success in combined task and compliance metrics. The study also finds that fine-tuning alone may not significantly improve normative competence, indicating a gap in AI's ability to acquire transferable social norms through interaction.

entry.title: Researchers propose LLM-based feature extraction to integrate unstructured customer feedback into multi-criteria inventory classification, enhancing prioritization in e-commerce supply chains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a method using large language models (LLMs) to extract quantitative features from unstructured data like customer reviews for multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) in e-commerce supply chains. Traditional methods rely mainly on structured data such as annual dollar usage, but this approach incorporates sentiment and other unstructured signals into the Hadi-Vencheh MCIC framework. Experimental results demonstrate that including customer sentiment leads to measurable changes in inventory classification, suggesting that leveraging unstructured data can improve inventory management decisions.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for test-time selection in LLMs, improving candidate solution choice by comparing options across multiple aspects without training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), a method for selecting the best candidate solution generated by large language models (LLMs) at test time. APT compares candidate solutions pairwise across multiple aspects using off-the-shelf verifiers, mimicking human decision-making by evaluating options aspect by aspect rather than in isolation. This approach improves performance over existing methods like binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency, and reward model verification, especially on open-ended tasks. APT operates as a single-elimination tournament where each matchup is decided by votes from multiple aspect verifiers, all specified in natural language. This design allows users to steer selection toward desired properties without retraining or regenerating solutions. The method transfers easily to new domains by rewriting prompts, requiring no additional training, and has been tested across five domains and three LLM generators with consistent improvements.

entry.title: Researchers present Forge Decision Context system to enable persistent behavioral learning in AI agents, improving compliance to 95% on a new benchmark with fewer tokens [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system designed to help large language model agents learn from human corrections and self-assessed failures across sessions by converting behavioral signals into imperative rules applied at relevant decision points. Evaluated on DC-Bench, a benchmark with 71 scenarios covering nine behavioral dimensions, forge_dc achieved 95% compliance compared to 55% with naive retrieval, while using about ten times fewer tokens per query. The study highlights that representing behavioral memory as explicit directives and delivering them at decision points are key design factors for effective persistent behavioral learning in AI agents.

entry.title: IWIBench benchmarks large editor models modifying smaller target models' weights without gradients across ten text-editing tasks, revealing uneven capabilities among leading models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: IWIBench is introduced as a benchmark to evaluate how well large editor models can modify the weights of smaller target models directly, without using gradients, to achieve various text-editing objectives while preserving other model functions. The benchmark tests ten classical editing tasks using limited tools and a fixed rollout budget, with a validator comparing edited models to unmodified versions in a clean environment. Evaluation of frontier closed- and open-weight models shows significant differences in performance across models and tasks, with Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol notably outperforming others, suggesting recent training improvements. Tasks vary in difficulty, with alias acquisition and recoding being more amenable to editing, while structured response and answer-length control proved challenging. Success in one task family does not strongly correlate with others, indicating an early and uneven development of intra-weight injection capabilities. The study discusses common editing strategies and positions intra-weight injection as a promising gradient-free method for modifying model behavior.

entry.title: Researchers compare debugger-only and bash-only coding agents on 500 SWE-bench instances using GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B models, introducing pass$_X$@$k$ to measure success probability across agents
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated the effectiveness of interactive debuggers versus bash tools for coding agents by comparing a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, using two large language models with multiple runs. They introduced pass$_X$@$k$, a metric estimating the probability that at least one of k agents succeeds, to distinguish interface specialization from sampling variance. The study found that differences in solved subsets were mainly due to run-to-run variance rather than complementary tool capabilities, with two bash rollouts outperforming a combination of bash and debugger rollouts. These findings emphasize the need to account for stochastic variance when assessing agent and tool diversity and propose pass$_X$@$k$ as a useful evaluation framework for the community.

entry.title: ChainFlow introduces a flow-matching drafter for speculative decoding that outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash on Qwen3.5 models by up to 39%, improving LLM inference speed [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: ChainFlow is a new speculative decoding method that accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target model's hidden states. Unlike existing drafters that either generate tokens one at a time or predict tokens independently, ChainFlow performs drafting as a short transport over hidden states with one or two flow steps, reducing computational cost and preserving inter-token dependencies. The approach uses a variational autoencoder to compress hidden states, lightweight feedback heads to restore token dependencies, and tree drafting to increase acceptance rates. On Qwen3.5 models, ChainFlow achieves 39% and 11% speed improvements over EAGLE-3 and DFlash drafters in vLLM, respectively, with gains increasing as drafters adapt to new languages. The authors provide ablation studies on drafter design and concurrent serving and have open-sourced their code and models.

entry.title: Researchers propose two optimal transport frameworks for backtracking counterfactual inference in Structural Causal Models, addressing exogenous variable distributions and independence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper studies backtracking counterfactual inference in Structural Causal Models (SCMs) using optimal transport methods. The authors introduce two frameworks that map the posterior distribution of exogenous variables, induced by factual observations, onto configurations satisfying counterfactual queries. One framework uses a pointwise projection suitable for direct use of the transported distribution, while the other enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables to maintain their interpretability as genuine noises of the SCM. The study demonstrates that both frameworks align with the original backtracking counterfactual principle and proposes several solvers for finite-posterior scenarios. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the problem's geometry and highlight trade-offs between transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

entry.title: Researchers find cancellation alone fails to restore service in overloaded vLLM engines with retries, delivering only 12-38% of calls after overload [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers tested cancellation and retry mechanisms on vLLM during overload experiments with three open models, tracking client attempts and engine executions. They found that retries often started shortly before timeout, leading to aborted executions that consumed most computed prompt tokens, while cancellation alone did not restore service and delivered a minority of calls after overload. The study showed that implementing a retry budget improved service by limiting retries but left many calls undelivered, whereas request coalescing delivered all calls post-overload unless cancellation had aborted execution. The findings suggest that overload controls should consider the additional executions caused by retries and the actual calls clients receive rather than relying solely on cancellation propagation.

entry.title: Researchers propose memory-aware multi-agent architecture with LLM-based orchestration for conversational recommendation, improving intent tracking and user acceptance in Amazon Reviews dataset experiments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation systems, where large language models (LLMs) orchestrate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow while integrating long-term memory to better capture evolving user intent. The system was evaluated on the Amazon Reviews dataset through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn simulations, and supervisor-driven studies, showing that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and increase user acceptance by nearly 29 percentage points. The study also identifies an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations, noting that while LLM-based reranking does not improve traditional Hit@K metrics, it enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To better measure these effects, the researchers introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), emphasizing the importance of system-level design choices such as explicit memory integration, structured orchestration, and evaluation beyond standard ranking metrics for effective conversational recommendation.

entry.title: Researchers propose AlterNet, a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with adaptive depth and learned halting for elastic inference in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce AlterNet, a novel large language model architecture combining Mixture-of-Experts with shallow experts and dynamic-depth mechanisms to adjust compute during inference. The model uses iterative computation, sequence-level depth routing with a halting mechanism, and depth encoding to track progress, enabling automatic compute allocation per task and post-training scaling without retraining. Initial benchmarks are presented alongside discussions of future research directions.

entry.title: AttentionSwitch jointly optimizes sparse attention-head selection and scaling to defend frozen large language models against jailbreak attacks, improving safety with limited training data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AttentionSwitch introduces a novel approach to defending large language models (LLMs) from jailbreak attacks by jointly learning which attention heads to intervene on and how to scale their outputs within a frozen model. This method allows selective amplification or attenuation of attention head outputs without changing their representation directions, addressing limitations of prior sequential optimization defenses. Evaluated across popular LLMs and jailbreak scenarios, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing methods, particularly when training data is scarce, offering a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning that avoids catastrophic forgetting.

entry.title: Researchers propose Debate-to-Deceive, a multi-agent game-theoretic framework that generates adversarial passages to poison LLM fact-checking, outperforming existing attacks on four benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework inspired by human rhetorical styles, designed to manipulate fact-checking judgments of large language models (LLMs). D2D models the adversarial process as an evolutionary game where agents adapt rhetorical strategies to produce semantically coherent and rhetorically effective adversarial content that resists early confirmation bias. D2D separates agent behavior into a strategic layer that selects rhetorical actions via evolutionary learning and a generation layer where the LLM produces passages based on these strategies and debate context. Evaluated on four fact-checking benchmarks-FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact-D2D significantly outperforms prior attack methods and evades most existing defenses, highlighting new challenges for AI reliability and robustness in fact-checking tasks.

entry.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

entry.title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.

entry.title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.

entry.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.

entry.title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.

entry.title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.

entry.title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.

entry.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.

entry.title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.

entry.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

entry.title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has been driven largely by scaling model size and human-curated training data, yet this paradigm is increasingly constrained by data scarcity and diminishing returns from human supervision. Self-play offers a promising pathway for autonomous data generation and improvement, but current frameworks remain unsatisfactory due to a lack of a data-centric perspective, limited cross-domain generalization, and growing trustworthiness and security concerns. In this paper, we argue that real-world LLM self-play systems should achieve effectiveness, generalizability, and trustworthiness under data scarcity. To address these challenges, we outline three blue-sky research directions for future self-play systems: (1) data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, (2) generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and (3) trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution. We further discuss research opportunities and solutions within each direction. This paradigm shift will establish a sustainable and safe AI ecosystem by transforming finite human knowledge into inexhaustible high-quality experience through self-play architectures.

entry.title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.

entry.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

entry.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

entry.title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

entry.title: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.08991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rare-event forecasting often depends on interpretable conjunctions: a single keyword, location, or temporal cue may be weak, while their joint occurrence can identify a meaningful precursor. Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (HTNL) selects Numerical Conjunctive Features (NCFs) through a structured sparsity objective. However, the resulting optimization problem is challenging, making optimization design critical to its practical performance. We give a unified diagnosis of four HTNL optimization families: original majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and weighted group lasso (WGL). Our analysis distinguishes three key factors that jointly determine HTNL optimization behavior. First, VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent under matched variational updates and optimize a squared-penalty formulation. Second, ADMM optimizes the unsquared objective through consensus splitting; we replace its truncated FISTA proximal solver with a scalar bisection update (ADMM-Bisect) for more accurate treatment of near-threshold blocks. Third, WGL targets the same unsquared objective, while all methods face rapidly decaying active-set admission scores. Across two synthetic datasets and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, VQF achieves the highest mean AUC with the most compact non-collapsing supports. ADMM-Bisect reduces measured runtime, while calibrated WGL avoids the empty-support failures of its original scale. Synthetic results further show how proximal accuracy, pruning, and search budget affect candidate recovery, especially for longer conjunctions. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

entry.title: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate traffic prediction is essential for urban planning but remains challenging due to the irregular patterns caused by unexpected events. While Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) effectively model periodic data, they often struggle with these aperiodic fluctuations. To address this, we propose SIMBAD, which improves generalization irregular patterns via two key mechanisms: 1) adaptive regulation of periodic signals to prioritize recent signals, and 2) dynamic spatial modeling that adjusts influence between connected nodes based on contextual relations. Built upon simple similarity metrics to adapt to aperiodic patterns, SIMBAD outperforms existing methods on real-world benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance in predicting unseen and irregular traffic events.

entry.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.

entry.title: CARGO: Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Preventive Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.

entry.title: BMMS: Policy-Conditioned Measurement of Behavioral Compliance in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Behavioral evaluation of language models fixes its dimensions in advance: hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity, over-refusal. An operator in a regulated industry needs a different question answered: does a system do what a particular rulebook requires? We introduce the Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (BMMS), which measures policy-conditioned misalignment by taking a policy corpus as an argument and returning a compliance profile over it, for any published policy and any system that answers in natural language. The Compliance Attainment Score (CAS) measures severity-weighted attainment over the obligations that bind the system, and the Compliance Robustness Margin (CRM) the share of that attainment surviving graded adversarial pressure; Behavioral Invariance (BIV) and the Behavioral Disposition Index (BDI) are specified and released with the suite. Dimensions enter only by passing a published admission test whose binding criterion is attribution: a quantity that moves when the judge changes, holding the target fixed, is measuring the instrument. Applying it excluded one of the quantities the suite itself reported. Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents in five registers, the admission criterion holds 94.4% precision against blinded human judgment on vendor specifications and 50.0% on analytical guidance, extraction fidelity is 94.6%, and re-scoring under judges from two other providers leaves target ordering invariant while the absolute score of a single target spans up to 0.22. We apply it to the two most detailed published behavioral specifications. Own-specification advantage is not resolved from zero once document difficulty is subtracted, but absolute self-compliance is another matter: GPT-4o fails 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in the Model Spec published by OpenAI, where the two Claude models fail 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.

entry.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.

entry.title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

entry.title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.

entry.title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.

entry.title: Large Language Model Consensus and Corpus-Adaptive Topic Modeling for Classifying and Mapping Patent Innovation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patent analytics increasingly relies on transformer representations and large language models (LLMs), yet linking conceptual classification, topic formation and interpretation requires explicit decisions about model roles and the evidence retained at each stage. In this design-oriented study, we propose and demonstrate a patent analytics pipeline that links these tasks and keeps each decision open to audit. Three LLMs separately classify each patent by novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process, service). Radical and innovation-type labels each require two supporting votes, with Incremental used as the fallback novelty label. Topics are discovered by clustering PatentSBERTa embeddings, with parameter ranges scaled to corpus size. A patent-specific stopword list is applied only when topics are represented with class-based term frequency--inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF), and a second embedding model supports inter-topic similarity, hierarchical refinement and visualization. An LLM then labels each topic from its ranked keywords and representative patents. We demonstrate the pipeline on 30,964 public-sector-related patents retrieved from Lens.org. Across five category corpora ranging from 591 to 29,215 patents, the pipeline produced 74 category-specific topic instances with a macro-average document coverage of 98.1% and topic diversity of 0.900--1.000, and fewer than 1% of classification outputs returned UNKNOWN. Because every model vote and the evidence behind each topic label are retained, analysts can audit and revise the outputs. The demonstration establishes the feasibility and traceability of the pipeline; testing its labels against expert coding and benchmarking it against alternative pipelines are identified as the next steps. The pipeline offers a reusable basis for LLM-assisted patent analysis in technology intelligence.

entry.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Option Shielding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.

entry.title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.

entry.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

entry.title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.

entry.title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.

entry.title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts. Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance. Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation. Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold. Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

entry.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

entry.title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.

entry.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

entry.title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.

entry.title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.

entry.title: Ontology-Driven Control of Conversational Agents with a Use-Case for Job Interview Practice [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used as conversational agents in both domain-specific and open-domain situations. In domain-specific context, it is often necessary to adapt those LLMs to obtain conversations with desired characteristics, whether those apply at the level of each response (e.g. for tone or style) or more globally (i.e. at the level of a conversational strategy). Such adaptations are, however, generally realized in an ad hoc way, through specific, non-reusable, and non-transparent developments. In this paper, we propose an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies that rely on the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances in the conversation.
